s0101.literal: The Last Emperor himself dwelt in the Linchun Pavilion; Precious Consort Zhang in the Jieqi Pavilion; the two honored consorts Gong and Kong in the Wangxian Pavilion; elevated passageways linked them so they could come and go to one another.
s0101.idiomatic: The Last Emperor lived in the Linchun Pavilion, Precious Consort Zhang in the Jieqi Pavilion, and Honored Consorts Gong and Kong in the Wangxian Pavilion, with skyways connecting them for constant visits.

s0102.literal: There were also the two Beautiful Ladies Wang and Li, the two Fair Ladies Zhang and Xue, Lady Yuan the Zhaoyi, Lady He the Jieyu, Lady Jiang the Xiurong, and seven others in all—all favored, taking turns to feast and roam upon the pavilions.
s0102.idiomatic: Seven more held favor—the Beautiful Ladies Wang and Li, the Fair Ladies Zhang and Xue, Zhaoyi Yuan, Jieyu He, and Xiurong Jiang—who took turns feasting and strolling on the terraces.

s0103.literal: Palace women of literary accomplishment, such as Yuan Dashe, were made female academicians.
s0103.idiomatic: Learned palace women such as Yuan Dashe were appointed female academicians.

s0104.literal: Whenever the Last Emperor led guests to feast with the Precious Consort and the others, he would have the various ladies and female academicians join intimates in composing new poems and exchanging verses; the most gorgeous were chosen for song lyrics, set to new tunes; palace women of pleasing looks were selected by the hundreds and thousands and made to study and sing them; [8] by sections they advanced in rotation, holding revel together.
s0104.idiomatic: Whenever the Last Emperor feasted with guests and the Precious Consort, he had the ladies and female academicians join familiar companions in new verse, trading lines; the finest were set as lyrics to new music, and hundreds or thousands of comely palace women were drilled to sing them—[8] sections took turns performing for the revel.

s0105.literal: Among the tunes were "Jade Tree, Rear-Court Blossom" and "Linchun Joy"; their drift in general praised the looks of Precious Consort Zhang and Honored Consort Kong.
s0105.idiomatic: Tunes such as "Jade Tree, Rear-Court Blossom" and "Linchun Joy" chiefly praised the beauty of Precious Consort Zhang and Honored Consort Kong.

s0106.literal: The gist runs: "The jade moon is full every night; the jeweled tree is fresh each dawn.
s0106.idiomatic: The gist runs: "The jade moon is full every night; the jeweled tree is fresh each dawn.

s0107.literal: " Yet Precious Consort Zhang's hair was seven feet long, black as lacquer, its luster mirror-bright.
s0107.idiomatic: " Precious Consort Zhang's hair was seven feet long, black as lacquer and bright enough to mirror one's face.

s0108.literal: Exceptionally clever and spirited, dignified in bearing, her countenance proper and lovely.
s0108.idiomatic: She was exceptionally clever and spirited, graceful in movement, with a proper and lovely face.

s0109.literal: Whenever she glanced or looked sidelong, brilliance overflowed her eyes and lit those on either side.
s0109.idiomatic: Each sidelong glance brimmed with light and lit the company around her.

s0110.literal: She often made up finely atop the pavilion and leaned from the balustrade; viewed from afar within the palace she seemed to drift like an immortal.
s0110.idiomatic: She often dressed at the pavilion rail; seen from afar in the palace she seemed to float like an immortal.

s0111.literal: Gifted in argument with a strong memory, skilled at reading the sovereign's mood.
s0111.idiomatic: Quick-witted and retentive, she was adept at reading the ruler's mood.

s0112.literal: At that time the Last Emperor neglected government; when the hundred offices submitted memorials they all reached him through the eunuchs Cai Tuo'er and Li Shandu; [9] he seated Precious Consort Zhang on his lap to decide them together.
s0112.idiomatic: The Last Emperor had grown slack in rule; memorials from every office came only through eunuchs Cai Tuo'er and Li Shandu—[9] and he set Precious Consort Zhang on his knee to decide them with him.

s0113.literal: What Li and Cai could not remember, the Precious Consort would set out in ordered lists, omitting nothing.
s0113.idiomatic: What Li and Cai forgot, the Precious Consort would lay out in clear lists without omission.

s0114.literal: Hence favor grew still more extraordinary; she stood above all the inner quarters.
s0114.idiomatic: Favor grew still more singular, and she stood first in the inner palace.

s0115.literal: When households of the inner palace broke the law and were at fault in principle, they need only plead with the Precious Consort; she would have Li and Cai first report the matter, then calmly speak for them.
s0115.idiomatic: Inner-palace families who broke the law would beg the Precious Consort's mercy; she had Li and Cai raise the case first, then spoke for them at leisure.

s0116.literal: If ministers did not comply, she would slander them too; nothing she said went unheard.
s0116.idiomatic: Ministers who resisted were slandered as well, and the ruler heard her every word.

s0117.literal: Thus the power of Zhang and Kong scorched all directions; ministers in charge also bowed before the wind.
s0117.idiomatic: Zhang and Kong's influence blazed everywhere, and ministers in power bent with the wind.

s0118.literal: Eunuchs and sycophants linked inside and outside, recommending one another in turn; bribes ran openly, rewards and punishments had no fixed rule, and order was utterly confused.
s0118.idiomatic: Eunuchs and flatterers joined court and harem, promoting one another; bribes were open, rewards and punishments erratic, and discipline collapsed.

s0119.literal: The historian says: The Odes praise the virtue of the ospreys; the Book of Changes sets forth the foundation of Heaven and Earth—yet the relation of husband and wife is the great constant of human conduct.
s0119.idiomatic: The historian writes: The Odes honor the virtue of the ospreys and the Changes lay the base of Heaven and Earth, yet marriage is the chief bond of human life.

s0120.literal: As for matching Heaven's pattern and harmonizing royal transformation, Queen Dowager Xuan had such virtue.
s0120.idiomatic: To pair with Heaven's norm and aid royal transformation—Queen Dowager Xuan had that excellence.

s0122.literal: Fair Lady Zhaorong / Lady Zhaoyi: in the Northern Supervisory, Ji, and Palace editions "Zhaoyi" stands above "Zhaorong."
s0122.idiomatic: On "Zhaorong, Zhaoyi": Northern Supervisory, Ji, and Palace editions place Zhaoyi above Zhaorong.

s0123.literal: Note: the preface to the "Biographies of Empresses and Consorts" in the History of the Southern Dynasties, on the nine consort ranks instituted by Emperor Wu of Liang, places "Zhaoyi" above "Zhaorong"; Chen institutions mostly followed Liang—the order Zhaoyi, Zhaorong is correct.
s0123.idiomatic: The Southern Dynasties preface to the consorts' biographies lists Liang's nine ranks with Zhaoyi above Zhaorong; Chen largely followed Liang, so Zhaoyi, Zhaorong is correct.

s0125.literal: [present] what is here compiled—changed according to all editions.
s0125.idiomatic: On "[present] what is here compiled": emended per all editions.

s0128.literal: [cheng] county marquis—changed according to the History of the Southern Dynasties.
s0128.idiomatic: On "[cheng] county marquis": emended per the History of the Southern Dynasties.

s0129.literal: Note: Jiancheng county was a Han marquisate.
s0129.idiomatic: Jiancheng county was a Han enfeoffment.

s0130.literal: The Universal Gazetteer cites Lei Cizong's Record of Yuzhang: "Emperor Gaodi of Han established it.
s0130.idiomatic: The Universal Gazetteer quotes Lei Cizong's Record of Yuzhang: "Emperor Gaodi of Han established it.

s0131.literal: Because he founded the city-settlement, it is called Jiancheng.
s0131.idiomatic: Because he founded the settlement, it was called Jiancheng.

s0132.literal: " In the present Han Treatise and tables it reads Jiancheng (built-complete); from the Later Han Treatise onward all read Jiancheng (establish-city).
s0132.idiomatic: " The Han Treatise and tables read Jiancheng (built-complete); from the Later Han Treatise on all read Jiancheng (establish-city).

s0133.literal: Later the younger brother of Empress Wen, Qin, inherited as Marquis of Jiancheng—there too it reads Jiancheng.
s0133.idiomatic: Later Empress Wen's brother Qin inherited as Marquis of Jiancheng, likewise written Jiancheng.

s0134.literal: "In the eleventh year of Daye died at the Eastern Capital"—note: the History of the Southern Dynasties reads twelfth year for eleventh.
s0134.idiomatic: On "died at the Eastern Capital in Daye year eleven": the History of the Southern Dynasties reads year twelve.

s0135.literal: "yet was deeply favored"—the character you in all editions reads you (by/from).
s0135.idiomatic: On "yet was deeply favored": all editions read you (by) for you (still).

s0136.literal: Note: you and you are interchangeable.
s0136.idiomatic: You and you are used interchangeably here.

s0137.literal: "In the third year of Taijian taken in as crown prince's consort"—note: on "third year of Taijian" one should follow
s0137.idiomatic: On "taken as crown prince's consort in Taijian year three": Taijian year three should follow

s0139.idiomatic: which reads first year of Taijian.

s0141.literal: says that in Taijian year two the High Ancestor made Junli's daughter crown prince's consort—this too is erroneous.
s0141.idiomatic: says the High Ancestor made Junli's daughter crown prince's consort in Taijian year two—that too is wrong.

s0142.literal: "Then before the Guangzhao Hall he raised the three pavilions Linchun, Jieqi, and Wangxian"—"Guangzhao Hall" in the Biography of Precious Consort Zhang in the History of the Southern Dynasties reads Guangzhao Hall; the Comprehensive Mirror agrees.
s0142.idiomatic: On "before Guangzhao Hall he raised Linchun, Jieqi, and Wangxian": the Southern Dynasties biography of Precious Consort Zhang and the Comprehensive Mirror read Guangzhao Hall.

s0143.literal: "ordered them to study and sing"—ge in the Palace edition reads ge (counter).
s0143.idiomatic: On "ordered them to study and sing": the Palace edition reads ge (unit) for ge (sing).

s0144.literal: Note: ge is the ancient graph for song.
s0144.idiomatic: Ge is the archaic form of the graph for song.

s0145.literal: "all through the eunuchs Cai Tuo'er and Li Shandu to present petitions"—"Cai Tuo'er" in the History of the Southern Dynasties reads Cai Lin'er.
s0145.idiomatic: On "memorials came through eunuchs Cai Tuo'er and Li Shandu": the History of the Southern Dynasties reads Cai Lin'er for Cai Tuo'er.
